Διατί οὖν, φημί, κύριε, ὡσεὶ ξηρά εἰσι καὶ ὅμοια; Ὅτι, φησίν, οὔτε οἱ δίκαιοι φαίνονται οὔτε οἱ ἁμαρτωλοὶ ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ, ἀλλ᾽ ὅμοιοί εἰσιν· ὁ γὰρ αἰὼν οὗτος τοῖς δικαίοις χειμών ἐστι, καὶ οὐ φαίνονται μετὰ τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν κατοικοῦντες. 3. ὥσπερ γὰρ ἐν τῷ χειμῶνι τὰ δένδρα ἀποβεβληκότα τὰ φύλλα ὅμοιά εἰσι, καὶ οὐ φαίνονται τὰ ξηρὰ ποῖά εἰσιν ἢ τὰ ζῶντα, οὕτως ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ οὐ φαίνονται οὔτε οἱ δίκαιοι οὔτε οἱ ἁμαρτωλοί, ἀλλὰ πάντες ὅμοιοί εἰσιν. translation.text:
…they make their wealth complete, and in turn the rich, by supplying the poor with the things they need, make their souls complete[a].

9. Thus both become partners in the work of righteousness. Therefore the one who does these things will not be abandoned by God, but will be inscribed in the books of the living[b].

10. Blessed are those who have and understand that they are made rich from the Lord; for those who think this way will be able to do some good.

Another parable.

1. He showed me many trees that had no leaves, but they seemed to me to be dry; for they were all alike. And he says to me, “Do you see these trees?” “I see,” I say, “sir[c], that they are alike and dry.” Answering, he says to me, “These trees that you see are those who dwell in this age[d].”

2. “Why then, sir, are they as if dry and alike?” I say. “Because,” he says, “neither the righteous nor the sinners are visible in this age, but they are alike; for this age is winter for the righteous, and they are not visible while dwelling among sinners.”

3. “For just as in winter the trees, having cast off their leaves, are alike, and it is not apparent which are dry or which are living, so in this age neither the righteous nor the sinners are apparent, but all are alike.”

Another parable.

1. He showed me again many trees, some sprouting and others dry, and he says to me, “Do you see these trees?” “I see,” I say, “sir, some sprouting and others dry.”

2. “These trees that are sprouting,” he says, “are the righteous, who are about to dwell in the age to come; for the age to come is summer for the righteous, but winter for sinners. Therefore when the mercy of the Lord shines forth, then those serving God will be made manifest, and all will be made manifest.”

3. “For just as in summer the fruits of each tree become visible and are recognized for what they are, so also the fruits of the righteous will be visible, and all will be known, [those who are least] being flourishing in that age[e].”

4. “But the nations[f] and the sinners—like the dry trees you saw—will be found such, dry and fruitless in that age, and as …[g]”

footnotes.text: The verb πληροφορέω can mean to bring something to full measure or fulfillment. In this context it contrasts material 'wealth' with the 'soul,' each being made complete through mutual support.
On the motif, compare Exod 32:32–33; Ps 69:28; Dan 12:1. Hermas’s wording is plural ('books of the living'), not the singular 'book of life.'
Greek κύριε here is respectful address to the visionary guide; 'sir' avoids confusion with the divine title 'Lord.'
Greek αἰών denotes an age or epoch. Hermas contrasts the present age (winter) with the coming age (summer).
Some witnesses include the words 'οἱ ἐλάχιστοι ὄντες' ('even the least'), which would read, 'and all—even the least—will be known as flourishing in that age.'
ἔθνη is rendered 'the nations' rather than 'Gentiles' to retain a broad, non-technical sense.

lexical_decisions.chosen: bring to full measure / make complete
lexical_decisions.rationale: In Koine this verb can mean to bring something to fulfillment or completion (cf. 2 Tim 4:5). Here it fits the reciprocal image: the poor (by implication) and the rich each bring something to completion—wealth and soul. 'Make complete' is clear and preserves the metaphorical fullness.
Common sense of providing for needs; 'supplying' keeps the concrete economic imagery.
Context is material aid to the poor. 'Necessities' conveys required provisions rather than moral propriety.
'Partners' communicates mutual participation in a shared work without softening the ethical dimension.
δικαίου here is moral righteousness rather than abstract justice; 'work of righteousness' keeps Hermas’s ethical tone.
Stock biblical idiom; 'abandoned' is clear and weighty.

lexical_decisions.source_word: ἐπιγεγραμμένος εἰς τὰς βίβλους τῶν ζώντων
lexical_decisions.chosen: inscribed in the books of the living
alternatives: written in the book of the living
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the plural 'books' and the phrase 'of the living.' Echoes a known motif without collapsing to the singular 'book of life.'
'Blessed' preserves the beatitude register and gravity.
Cognitive grasp of the source of wealth is in view.

lexical_decisions.chosen: are made rich from the Lord
lexical_decisions.rationale: Passive divine agency; 'from the Lord' keeps the prepositional nuance (παρά).
Ethical mindset language common in early Christian paraenesis.
Keeps the concrete imagery of working good rather than abstract 'do good.'
Address is to the visionary’s guide, not to God. 'Sir' avoids conflation with the divine title 'Lord.'
Hermas contrasts present and coming 'ages' (temporal horizons), not cosmos vs. inhabited world. 'Age' preserves apocalyptic temporal frame.
Seasonal metaphor is explicit and vivid; 'winter'/'summer' are natural choices.
Light metaphor attached to mercy; 'shines out' keeps the concrete image.
While the verb connotes slavery, here the focus is on manifest service; 'serving God' reads smoothly without importing the full 'slave' metaphor.

lexical_decisions.chosen: fruits … are recognized what sort they are
alternatives: fruits … are found of what kind they are
fruits … are known what quality they are
lexical_decisions.rationale: Keeps the evaluative nuance of ποταπός with the recognition verb.
Common arboreal/vitality metaphor; 'flourishing' fits the tree imagery and moral vigor.
'The nations' is the broad, non-technical term; 'Gentiles' risks later Christian ethnoreligious connotations not demanded here.
'Fruitless' aligns with the tree/fruit metaphor already in use.

theological_decisions.issue: Rendering κύριος (voc.) in dialogue with the angelic shepherd
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Translate κύριε as 'sir' in this context
theological_decisions.rationale: The addressee is the visionary guide, not God. Using 'sir' prevents confusion with the divine title while preserving respectful address.

theological_decisions.issue: Eschatological contrast of αἰών (present vs. coming)
theological_decisions.rationale: Hermas contrasts temporal epochs (now vs. coming). 'Age' cleanly conveys this without cosmological overtones of 'world' or the opacity of 'aeon.'

theological_decisions.issue: 'Books of the living' vs. traditional 'book of life'
theological_decisions.rationale: The Greek is plural and says 'of the living.' Retaining it preserves Hermas’s diction and avoids importing later or different phrasing.

alternative_readings: 'Slaves of God' to emphasize doulos imagery
theological_decisions.rationale: Although the root can carry slavery imagery, here the focus is disclosure of allegiance ('those serving God'). 'Serving' communicates allegiance without over-specifying social metaphor.
Hermas’s paraenesis leans toward moral righteousness language; 'righteous' keeps the moral-ascetical tone and avoids juridical narrowing.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Take 'have' as material possession and render the clause, 'those who have and understand that from the Lord they are made rich'
alternative_readings: Generalize 'have' to any gift or capacity
theological_decisions.rationale: Context speaks of rich supplying necessities to the poor. Thus 'have' naturally refers to those possessing means.
'The nations' is the least anachronistic and widest term; Hermas’s contrast is moral (righteous vs. sinners) rather than insider/outsider to Israel.

review_passes.summary: The translation is excellent. It accurately captures the Greek source, maintains the appropriate register, and handles the textual fragment at the end perfectly. No changes are necessary.

And he says to me, “Do you see these trees?” “I see,” I say, “sir, that they are alike and dry.” Answering, he says to me, “These trees that you see are those who dwell in this age.”
